p.src: Let us say no more for now of Elder Tang's sufferings. Now the three demon chiefs, united in purpose and exerting all their strength, fought fiercely with the Great Sage and his two brothers halfway up the mountain east of the city. This battle was truly an iron brush scrubbing a copper pot—every one of them unyieldingly hard. What a deadly fight it was:

p.src: The six fought for a long while, until gradually evening fell. Wind and mist spread all around, and in an instant it was dark. Bajie's great ears drooped over his eyelids, making his sight dimmer still; his hands and feet slowed, and he could no longer parry the blows, so he dragged his rake away and fled in defeat. The eldest demon swung his blade at him and nearly took his life. Luckily he ducked his head; the demon's beak-blade merely sliced off several bristles. Catching up, the demon opened his mouth, seized Bajie by the collar, carried him into the city, and threw him to the lesser demons, who bound him in the Golden Throne Hall. The eldest demon then mounted the clouds again and rose into the air to lend his aid. Seeing that matters had gone awry, Monk Sha feinted with his precious staff, turned to save himself, and fled. But the second demon thrust out his trunk and, with a resounding snap, wrapped him up together with his arms. He carried him into the city and likewise ordered the lesser demons to bind him below the hall. Then he soared back into the air, calling for the others to capture Pilgrim.

p.src: When Pilgrim saw both his brothers captured, he knew he could not hold out alone. As the saying goes: even a fine fighter cannot withstand two fists, and two fists cannot withstand four hands. With a shout he swept aside the three demons' weapons with his cudgel, turned a somersault, mounted the clouds, and fled. When the third demon saw Pilgrim turn his somersault, he shook himself, revealed his true form, spread his two wings, and pursued the Great Sage. You may wonder how he could catch him. When Pilgrim once caused havoc in Heaven, even a hundred thousand celestial troops could not capture him, for his somersault cloud carried him one hundred and eight thousand li at a bound, and thus none of the gods could overtake him. But this demon could cover ninety thousand li with one beat of his wings, so with two beats he passed him. Thus the demon seized him in one grasp and held him fast, so that he could not struggle free however he twisted. He longed to escape, but there was no way to get free. Even his arts of transformation and escape were useless: if he grew larger, the demon loosened his grip to hold him; if he grew smaller, the demon tightened his grasp. The demon carried him straight back into the city, released his grip, and flung him down into the dust. He ordered the assembled demons to bind him together with Bajie and Monk Sha. The eldest and second demons both came down to welcome him, and the three demon chiefs entered the treasure hall together. Ah! This time they had not truly bound Pilgrim at all; they had plainly come to see him on his way.

p.src: It was now around the second watch. When all the demons had finished assembling and greeting one another, they pushed Tang Sanzang down from the hall. By the lamplight the elder suddenly saw all three disciples bound on the floor. The old master threw himself beside Pilgrim and wept, saying, “Disciple! Whenever we met with danger before, you would be outside employing your divine powers, going here or there to seek help and subdue the demons. But now that you too have been captured, how can this poor monk survive?” Hearing their master's anguish, Bajie and Monk Sha also burst into bitter tears. Pilgrim smiled faintly and said, “Master, set your mind at ease; brothers, do not cry. Whatever they may do, we shall certainly come to no harm. Once the eldest demon has settled down, we shall be on our way.” Bajie said, “Brother, you are up to your tricks again. We are bound with hempen ropes, and whenever they slacken, the demons spray them with water. A skinny fellow like you may not feel it, but a fat one like me is suffering terribly. If you do not believe me, look at my arms—the ropes have already bitten two inches into the flesh. How can I get free?” Pilgrim laughed. “Never mind hempen rope—even a palm-fiber hawser as thick as a bowl would be no more to me than an autumn breeze passing my ears. What is there to marvel at?”

p.src: While master and disciples were speaking, they heard the eldest demon say, “Third brother is both mighty and clever. His excellent plan has indeed succeeded in capturing Tang Sanzang.” He called out, “Underlings! Have five of you fetch water, seven scrub the pot, ten tend the fire, and twenty carry out the iron steamer. Steam those four monks until they are cooked, so that we brothers may enjoy them. We shall also distribute a piece to each of you, so that every one of you may attain long life.” When Bajie heard this, he trembled and said, “Brother, listen! The demons are planning to steam and eat us.” Pilgrim said, “Do not be afraid. Let me see whether they are novice demons or skilled ones.” Monk Sha wept, “Brother, do not boast so lightly. We are already next door to King Yama, so what is the use of talking about ‘novices’ and ‘experts’?” Before he had finished speaking, they heard the second demon say, “Zhu Bajie will be hard to steam.” Bajie rejoiced. “Amitabha! Which virtuous soul said I was hard to steam?” The third demon said, “If he is hard to steam, skin him first and then steam him.” Bajie panicked and shouted at the top of his voice, “Do not skin me! Tough though I am, once the broth boils, I shall soon become tender.” The eldest demon said, “Put whatever is hard to steam on the lowest tier.” Pilgrim laughed. “Do not be afraid, Bajie. They are novices, not experts.” Monk Sha asked, “How can you tell?” Pilgrim said, “Whenever things are steamed, they cook from the top downward. Whatever is hard to steam should be placed in the top tier; stoke the fire well, and once the steam circulates fully, it will be cooked. But if it is placed at the bottom, it blocks the steam, and even after half a year of firing, the vapor will still not rise. They say Bajie is hard to steam yet would put him at the bottom—what can they be but novices?” Bajie said, “Brother, by your account they will torment a man to death while he is still alive. When they see the steam is not rising, what if they lift the steamer, turn me over, and light the fire again? Would they not cook both my sides through without leaving the middle raw?”

p.src: As they spoke, another lesser demon came to report, “The water is boiling.” The eldest demon gave the order to carry them over. The demons all set to work, carrying Bajie to the lowest tier and Monk Sha to the second. Pilgrim reckoned they were coming to carry him next, so he slipped free and thought, “This lamplight is a fine place to work my tricks.” He plucked out a hair, breathed an immortal breath upon it, and cried, “Change!” It instantly became another Pilgrim, bound with hempen rope. His true self left his spirit-form behind, leapt into the air, and looked down from above. The demons could not tell true from false. Seeing a body, they simply picked it up and carried the false Pilgrim to the third tier from the bottom. Then they knocked Tang Sanzang over, bound him, and carried him to the fourth tier. They piled up dry firewood, and fierce flames blazed high. From the clouds the Great Sage sighed, “My Bajie and Monk Sha could endure a couple of boils, but my master would fall apart after only one. If I do not use some magic to save him, he will perish in moments.”

p.src: The good Pilgrim formed a hand seal in midair and recited the spell, “Om, Lam, Pure Dharma Realm; Qian, origin, prosperity, benefit, constancy,” summoning the Dragon King of the Northern Sea, who arrived at once. A dark cloud appeared amid the clouds, and a voice called loudly in answer, “Ao Shun, humble dragon of the Northern Sea, bows before you.” Pilgrim said, “Rise, rise. I would not dare trouble you without cause. Master Tang and I came here, only to be captured by vicious demons, who have put him in an iron steamer. Go and protect him for me, and do not let him be ruined by the steaming.” The Dragon King immediately transformed himself into a blast of cold wind, blew beneath the pot, and circled around it protectively. No heat from the fire could reach the pot, and thus the three of them were spared from death.

p.src: As the third watch was drawing to its end, they heard the old demon issue orders: “Minions, by exerting ourselves and using strategy, we have captured Tang Sanzang and his three companions; and after the hardship of escorting them here, we have gone four days and nights without sleep. Now that they are bound inside the steamer, they are unlikely to escape. Keep careful watch, and have ten little demons tend the fire in shifts while we retire to the palace and get a little sleep. By the fifth watch, when dawn is near, they will surely be cooked tender. Prepare mashed garlic, salt, and vinegar, then wake us to enjoy them on empty stomachs.” The demons all obeyed. The three demon chiefs then returned to their respective sleeping chambers.

p.src: From the clouds, the Pilgrim heard every word of these orders. He lowered his cloud, but heard no voices from inside the steamer. He thought, “The heat from the fire rises, so it must be hot in there. Why are they not afraid, and why do they neither speak nor groan? Can they have been steamed to death? Let me go closer and listen again.” What a splendid Great Sage! Riding his cloud, he shook himself and changed into a black fly. He alighted outside the iron steamer’s bars and listened, hearing Bajie say from within, “What rotten luck! I cannot tell whether we are being steamed sealed tight or steamed with a vent.” Sha Monk asked, “Second Brother, what do you mean by ‘steamed sealed tight’ and ‘steamed with a vent’?” Bajie replied, “Steaming sealed tight means the lid is on the steamer; steaming with a vent means it is left off.” From the upper tier where he floated, Tripitaka called back, “Disciple, it has not been covered.” Bajie said, “What good fortune! We will not die tonight after all. We are being steamed with a vent.” Hearing all three of them speak and knowing they were still alive, the Pilgrim flew away and gently placed the lid on the iron steamer. Tripitaka cried in alarm, “Disciple, the lid has been put on!” Bajie said, “We are finished! Now we are being steamed sealed tight. We are sure to die tonight.” Sha Monk and the elder whimpered and wept. Bajie said, “Stop crying for now. The fire tenders have just changed shifts.” Sha Monk asked, “How do you know?” Bajie replied, “When they first carried us up here, it was just what I wanted. I suffer a little from cold and damp, and I wanted them to warm me through. But now I feel cold air coming up instead. Hey! Officers tending the fire, what would it hurt to add some more wood? Would it cost you anything?”

p.src: Hearing this, the Pilgrim could not suppress a silent laugh. “What a fool! Cold can still be endured, but heat would cost him his life. If he calls out another couple of times, he is sure to give us away. I had better rescue them quickly. Wait—if I am to rescue them, I must reveal my true form. If I do, these ten fire tenders will see me and raise a clamor together, alarming the old monsters. Would that not cause more trouble? Let me first send them a little magic.” Suddenly he remembered: “When I was the Great Sage, I once played finger-guessing games with the Heaven-Supporting King at the Northern Gate of Heaven and won some sleep-inducing insects from him. I still have a few; I will give them to these fellows.” He felt inside the pouch at his waist and found twelve still there. “I will give them ten and keep two for breeding.” He tossed the insects out, scattering them over the faces of the ten little demons. They crawled into their nostrils, and gradually the demons nodded off and all fell asleep. Only one, who held a fire fork, slept uneasily. He rubbed his head and face, pinched his nose this way and that, and sneezed without cease. The Pilgrim said, “This rogue has realized something is afoot. I will give him a double-wicked lamp.” He tossed another insect onto the fellow’s face. “With two insects, one entering from the left and leaving from the right, and the other leaving from the right and entering from the left, surely one of them will settle down.” The little demon gave two or three enormous yawns, stretched his back, dropped the fire fork, and fell forward asleep, never stirring again.

p.src: The Pilgrim said, “This magic is wondrous indeed, and truly effective.” He resumed his original form, approached, and called, “Master!” Tang Sanzang heard him and cried, “Wukong, save me!” Sha Monk said, “Elder Brother, is that you calling from outside?” The Pilgrim replied, “If I were not outside, would I be in there suffering with you?” Bajie said, “Brother, the nimble one slipped away, while we took the blame and are being stifled in here.” The Pilgrim laughed. “Fool, stop shouting. I have come to save you.” Bajie said, “Brother, if you save us, save us once and for all. Do not let us be put back in the steamer again.” The Pilgrim lifted the steamer lid and released his master. Then he shook the hairs he had transformed as decoys and gathered them back onto his body; then, tier by tier, he released Sha Monk and Bajie. The moment the fool was freed, he could hardly wait to run. The Pilgrim said, “Not so fast, not so fast.” He recited an incantation and dismissed the dragon spirit, then said to Bajie, “There are still lofty mountains and steep ridges on our westward journey. Master cannot travel without a mount. Wait while I fetch the horse.”

p.src: See how softly and stealthily he walked beneath the Golden Throne Hall, where he found all the demons, great and small, fast asleep. He untied the reins without disturbing anyone. The horse was actually a dragon horse. Had a stranger approached, it would have lashed out twice with its hind legs and whinnied several times. But the Pilgrim had once tended horses and held the office of Protector of the Horses, and besides, they belonged to the same party; so the horse neither kicked nor cried out. He quietly led it back, tightened the girth, made the tack secure, and invited his master to mount. Trembling, the elder mounted and was eager to leave. The Pilgrim said, “Let us not hurry yet. On our westward way we must still pass through kingdoms, and we need the travel rescript before we can proceed; otherwise, what credentials could we present? Wait while I go back and find the luggage.” Tang Sanzang said, “I remember that when we entered, the monsters put the luggage to the left of the Golden Hall. The carrying pole was there too.” The Pilgrim replied, “I understand.” He turned away and leapt into the jeweled hall to search, when suddenly he saw a wavering radiance. The Pilgrim knew it came from their luggage. How did he know? Tang Sanzang’s brocade cassock was set with a night-shining pearl, and it was this that gave off the light. He hurried forward and found that the carrying load was still sealed and untouched. He quickly took it away and handed it to Sha Monk to carry.

p.src: Bajie led the horse, while the Pilgrim led the way straight toward the Zhengyang Gate. They heard the warning clappers and bells ring out in a confusion. The gate was locked, with an official seal pasted over the lock. The Pilgrim said, “With defenses like these, how can we get out?” Bajie said, “Let us go out by the rear gate.” The Pilgrim led the way straight to the rear gate, but outside the Rear Slaughter Gate there was also the sound of warning clappers and bells, and that gate too was sealed and locked. “What are we to do now? If Tang Sanzang were not a mortal, the three of us could leave without difficulty, riding clouds and commanding the wind. But Tang Sanzang has not transcended the Three Realms and still remains within the Five Elements. His whole body is made of the impure bones inherited from his parents, so he cannot rise and ride the clouds, and escape is difficult.” Bajie said, “Brother, there is no need to discuss it. Let us find a place without warning clappers or guards, lift Master up, and climb over the wall.” The Pilgrim laughed. “That would not do. Helpless as we are, we might lift him over now; but when we return after obtaining the scriptures, you, loose-tongued fool, will tell everyone wherever we go that we are wall-climbing monks.” Bajie said, “At a time like this, we cannot worry about propriety. Let us save our lives first.” The Pilgrim had no other choice, so he agreed. They went to a clear stretch of wall and planned how to climb out.

The Pilgrim said, “With defenses like these, how can we get out?”
Bajie said, “Let us go out by the rear gate.”
The Pilgrim led the way straight to the rear gate, but outside the Rear Slaughter Gate there was also the sound of warning clappers and bells, and that gate too was sealed and locked.
“What are we to do now?

p.src: Alas! That such a thing should happen showed that Tripitaka's baleful star had not yet passed. The three demon chiefs were sleeping in the palace when they suddenly awoke with a start. Saying that the Tang Monk had escaped, they threw on their clothes, hurriedly rose, and rushed to the throne hall. They asked, “How many times has the Tang Monk come to the boil?” The little demons tending the fire had already been visited by the sleep insects and were all fast asleep; even a beating could not have roused a single one. A few of the others who were off duty awoke in alarm and stammered heedlessly, “S-s-s-seven times.” They raced to the cauldron and saw the steamer trays scattered over the ground while the fire tenders still slept. In panic they returned to report, “Your Majesties, he’s e-e-e-escaped!” All three demon chiefs descended from the hall and inspected the cauldron closely. Sure enough, the steamer trays lay scattered on the ground, the water in the pot was cold, and every trace of fire was gone. The fire tenders were all snoring away, dead to the world. In consternation the monsters all raised a cry: “Quick, seize the Tang Monk! Quick, seize the Tang Monk!” The clamor rang out and roused every demon, front and rear, great and small. Brandishing swords and spears, they swarmed to the Zhengyang Gate. They found the locks undisturbed and the watch clappers and bells sounding without cease. They asked the night patrol outside, “Where did the Tang Monk escape from?” They all replied, “No one came out.” They hurried to the rear service gate, but its locks, clappers, and bells were just as at the front gate. Then they rushed about with lanterns and torches until the sky glowed red as day, and plainly caught sight of the four pilgrims climbing the wall. The eldest demon rushed up and shouted, “Where do you think you’re going?” The elder was so terrified that his legs weakened and his sinews went numb. He tumbled from the wall and was seized by the eldest demon. The second demon caught Sha Monk, the third overpowered Bajie, and the lesser demons seized the luggage and the white horse. Only the Pilgrim escaped. Bajie grumbled and muttered, blaming the Pilgrim: “Damn him! I said that if he meant to save us, he should save us once and for all. Now we’re going back into the steamer again.”

p.src: The demons dragged the Tang Monk to the hall, but did not steam him again. The second demon ordered Bajie bound to a pillar beneath the front eaves, and the third ordered Sha Monk bound to a pillar beneath the rear eaves; only the eldest demon held the Tang Monk tightly and would not let go. The third demon said, “Elder Brother, why are you holding him like that? Surely you do not mean to eat him alive? There would be no savor in that. This creature is not like some ignorant commoner whom one may simply seize and eat as a meal; he is a rare delicacy from the superior land. We must wait for a cloudy day when we are at leisure, bring him out, prepare him with exquisite cleanliness, play drinking games, and consume him slowly with music and ceremony. Only that will do.” The eldest demon laughed. “What you say is right, worthy brother, but Sun the Pilgrim will come stealing him again.” The third demon said, “Inside this imperial palace there is a Pavilion of Brocaded Fragrance, and within it stands an iron chest. Do as I suggest: hide the Tang Monk in the chest and lock the pavilion; then spread a rumor that we have eaten him half raw, and order the lesser demons to tell it throughout the city. The Pilgrim is certain to come seeking news. Once he hears this, he will lose all hope and leave for good. If he does not return to trouble us for three or five days, we can bring the monk out and enjoy him at our leisure. What do you say?” The eldest and second demons were delighted. “Yes, yes, yes! Our brother speaks good sense.” Poor Tang Monk was taken inside that very night, hidden in the chest, and the pavilion was shut; then the rumor was spread and repeated wildly throughout the city, but of that no more need be said.

p.src: Now the Pilgrim, unable to look after the Tang Monk after midnight, had escaped on his cloud. He went straight to Lion-Camel Cave and, sweeping through with his cudgel, utterly exterminated its tens of thousands of lesser demons. He hurried back as the sun rose in the east. Reaching the city’s edge, he dared not issue a challenge. Just as the saying goes: one strand makes no thread, and one hand cannot clap. He descended from his cloud, shook himself, and changed into a little demon. Slipping through the gate, he searched every avenue and alley for news. Everyone in the city said that the kings had eaten the Tang Monk half raw during the night. Wherever he went, he heard the same story. The Pilgrim grew desperately anxious. When he reached the Golden Throne Hall and looked around, he saw many spirits inside. All wore gold-trimmed leather caps and long yellow robes, carried red-lacquered staves, and had ivory tablets hanging at their waists. They bustled endlessly to and fro. The Pilgrim thought, “These must be demons permitted to move through the palace. I’ll take their appearance and go inside to make inquiries.”

p.src: Dear Great Sage! He made himself identical in every respect and slipped through the golden gate. As he went along, he saw Bajie tied to a pillar before the hall, groaning. The Pilgrim went near and called, “Wuneng.” Recognizing the voice, the fool said, “Elder Brother, have you come? Please save me.” The Pilgrim said, “I will save you. Do you know where Master is?” Bajie said, “Master is gone. Last night the demons ate him half raw.” Hearing this, the Pilgrim suddenly broke down, and his tears gushed like a spring. Bajie said, “Brother, don’t cry. I only heard the little demons babbling about it; I did not see it myself. Do not let this delay you. Go and ask around again.” Only then did the Pilgrim check his tears and go farther inside to search. Suddenly he saw Sha Monk tied to a pillar beneath the rear eaves. Going up, he felt his chest and called, “Wujing.” Sha Monk also recognized the voice and said, “Elder Brother, have you come in by transforming yourself? Save me, save me.” The Pilgrim said, “Saving you is easy. Do you know where Master is?” Sha Monk shed tears and said, “Brother, the demons could not wait for Master to be steamed, so they ate him half raw.”

p.src: In utter misery the Pilgrim brooded, questioning his own heart: “All this is because our Buddha Tathagata sat there in the Land of Bliss with nothing to do and concocted those scriptures of the Tripitaka. If he truly wished to exhort people to goodness, he should have sent them to the Eastern Land. Would they not then have been handed down for all eternity? But he begrudged sending them and instead made us come to fetch them. How could he know that after suffering across a thousand mountains, we would come here today only for Master to lose his life? Enough, enough, enough! Old Sun will mount his somersault cloud, go before the Tathagata, and tell him the whole story. If he will let me carry the scriptures to the Eastern Land, they may, first, spread the fruits of goodness and, second, fulfill our cherished wish; but if he refuses, I shall have him recite the Spell for Loosening the Fillet, remove this circlet, and give it back to him. Then Old Sun will return to his own cave, proclaim himself king, call himself sovereign, and enjoy himself.”

p.src: The Great Sage promptly wheeled about, mounted his somersault cloud, and sped straight toward India. In less than an hour, he could already see that Spirit Mountain was near. In a moment he lowered his cloud and came directly beneath Vulture Peak. Suddenly he looked up and saw the Four Great Vajra Kings barring his way. “Where do you think you are going?” they demanded. The Pilgrim saluted them and said, “I have urgent business with the Tathagata.” Then the foremost of them, the Ever-Abiding Vajra, Indestructible Honored King of Golden Cloud Ridge on Mount Kunlun, shouted, “This macaque is outrageously rude! When you were hard pressed by the Bull Demon, we exerted ourselves on your behalf; yet today, meeting us face-to-face, you show no courtesy whatsoever. If you have business, wait while we first report it; enter only when summoned. This place is not like the Southern Gate of Heaven, where you are allowed to go in and out and rampage about on either side! Hey! Stand back at once!” The Great Sage was already in the depths of distress, and this rebuke only added to it. So furious was he that he roared like thunder, and, unable to restrain himself, began shouting at the top of his voice. His clamor soon alarmed the Tathagata.

p.src: The Buddha Tathagata was seated upright upon his jeweled lotus throne of nine tiers, expounding the scriptures to the eighteen Arhats who take turns descending into the world. He immediately said, “Sun Wukong has arrived. Go out and receive him.” Obeying the Buddha’s decree, the assembled Arhats went out through the mountain gate in two ranks, with banners, streamers, and jeweled canopies, and called, “Great Sage Sun, the Tathagata has summoned you.” Only then did the Four Great Vajra Kings at the mountain gate step aside and let the Pilgrim pass. The Arhats led him beneath the jeweled lotus throne. At the sight of the Tathagata, he prostrated himself, tears streaming from both eyes as he sobbed. The Tathagata asked, “Wukong, what has happened to make you weep so bitterly?” The Pilgrim replied, “Your disciple has repeatedly received the grace of your instruction and has found shelter beneath the Buddha’s protection. Since returning to the righteous path, I have protected the Tang Monk and revered him as my master; the hardships along the way have been beyond telling. Now, at Lion Camel Mountain, Lion Camel Cave, and Lion Camel City, there are three vicious demons—the Lion King, the Elephant King, and the Great Peng. They captured my master, and all of us disciples met with disaster as well: we were bound inside steamers to suffer boiling water and fire. Fortunately, I escaped and summoned the Dragon Kings, who saved the others from that fate. That night I secretly brought my master and the others out, but ill fortune would not release us, and they were captured once more. At daybreak I entered the city to make inquiries, only to learn that the intolerably cruel and ferocious demon had eaten my master half raw during the night. Now neither flesh nor bones remain. Moreover, my junior brothers Wuneng and Wujing are still bound over there, and before long their lives too will surely be lost. There was nothing your disciple could do, so I came here expressly to pay homage to the Tathagata. I beg you in your great mercy to recite the Spell for Loosening the Fillet, remove this band from my head, and let me return it to you; then release your disciple to go back to Flower-Fruit Mountain and live there at ease, amusing myself.” Before he had finished speaking, his tears gushed like a spring, and his lamentations would not cease. The Tathagata smiled and said, “Wukong, do not distress yourself so. That demon possesses vast supernatural powers. You could not defeat him, and that is why you are so heartsick.” Still kneeling below, the Pilgrim beat his chest and said, “I will conceal nothing from the Tathagata. In former years your disciple caused havoc in Heaven and styled himself Great Sage. Since I first came into the world, I had never suffered defeat—until now, when I fell into the hands of these vicious demons.”

p.src: Hearing this, the Tathagata said, “Put aside your resentment for now. I know that demon.” The Pilgrim suddenly blurted out, “Tathagata, I have heard people say that the demon is a relative of yours!” The Tathagata said, “You mischievous macaque! In what way is that demon related to me?” The Pilgrim laughed. “If he were not related to you, how would you know him?” The Tathagata replied, “I beheld him with my wisdom eye, and that is how I know him. The eldest and second demons both have masters.” He called, “Ananda and Kasyapa, come here. Separately mount your clouds and go to Mount Wutai and Mount Emei, and summon Manjusri and Samantabhadra to appear before me.” The two venerable disciples immediately departed in obedience to his command. The Tathagata said, “Those two are the masters of the eldest and second demons. As for the third demon, when the matter is explained, there is indeed some kinship between him and me.” The Pilgrim asked, “Is he kin on your father’s side— or your mother’s?” The Tathagata said, “When primal chaos first divided, Heaven opened in the Rat hour, Earth was formed in the Ox hour, and humankind arose in the Tiger hour. Heaven and Earth then joined once more, and all living things were born. Among living things were beasts that walked and birds that flew. The qilin was chief of the beasts, and the phoenix chief of the birds. The phoenix in turn received the generative essence of union and gave birth to the Peacock and the Great Peng. When the Peacock first came into the world, she was exceedingly savage and could devour human beings. From forty-five li away, she could suck a person into her mouth in a single breath. While I was atop the Snow Mountain, having perfected my sixteen-foot golden body, she swallowed me into her belly as well. I considered leaving by her lower passage, but feared that it would defile my true body. So I split open her back and ascended to Spirit Mountain. I meant to take her life, but all the Buddhas dissuaded me, saying that to harm the Peacock would be like harming my own mother. I therefore kept her at the assembly on Spirit Mountain and conferred upon her the title Bodhisattva, Peacock Great Wisdom King, Mother of Buddhas. The Great Peng was born of the same mother as the Peacock, and that is why there is some kinship between us.” Hearing this, the Pilgrim laughed. “Tathagata, if the relationship is reckoned that way, then you are actually the demon’s nephew!” The Tathagata said, “I must go in person before that monster can be subdued.” The Pilgrim kowtowed and petitioned the Tathagata: “I earnestly beg Your Reverence to deign to make the journey.”

There they met Ananda and Kasyapa returning with Manjusri and Samantabhadra. The two Bodhisattvas bowed before the Buddha. The Tathagata asked, “How long have your beasts been away from the mountain?” Manjusri replied, “Seven days.” The Tathagata said, “Only seven days have passed in the mountains, but several thousand years have gone by in the mortal world. Who knows how many living creatures they have harmed there? Quickly follow me to subdue them.” The two Bodhisattvas took their places on either side of him, and together with the assembly they flew through the sky. And this is what could be seen:

p.src: Through the Great Sage’s good connections, he had succeeded in inviting the Buddha and the whole assembly to come. Before long, the city walls were already in sight. The Pilgrim reported, “Tathagata, the place giving off that black vapor is the kingdom of Lion Camel.” The Tathagata said, “Go down first, enter the city, and engage the demons in battle. You are permitted to lose, but not to win. When you retreat up here in defeat, I shall subdue them myself.”

u.src: Through the Great Sage’s good connections, he had succeeded in inviting the Buddha and the whole assembly to come. Before long, the city walls were already in sight.
The Pilgrim reported, “Tathagata, the place giving off that black vapor is the kingdom of Lion Camel.”
The Tathagata said, “Go down first, enter the city, and engage the demons in battle. You are permitted to lose, but not to win.
When you retreat up here in defeat, I shall subdue them myself.”

p.src: The Great Sage immediately lowered his cloud, went straight to the city wall, planted his feet upon a battlement, and cursed, “You vile beasts! Come out at once and fight Old Sun!” The little fiends atop the gate tower were so alarmed that they hurried down into the city and reported, “Your Majesties, Sun the Pilgrim is on the wall challenging us to battle.” The eldest demon said, “That monkey has not come for two or three days, yet this morning he challenges us again. Could he have brought reinforcements?” The third demon said, “Why should we fear him? Let us all go and see.” Each of the three demon chiefs took up his weapon and rushed onto the wall. The moment they saw the Pilgrim, they spoke not a word but raised their weapons and thrust at him all together in wild disorder; the Pilgrim swung his iron staff and met them blow for blow. After fighting for seven or eight rounds, the Pilgrim feigned defeat and fled. With a thunderous shout, the demon kings cried, “Where do you think you are going?” The Great Sage sprang into a somersault and leapt high into the air; the three fiends mounted their clouds and gave chase. The Pilgrim slipped aside and hid within the golden radiance of the venerable Buddha, vanishing completely from sight. Then the three honored Buddhas of Past, Future, and Present, together with five hundred arhats and three thousand guardian deities, spread out to either side and surrounded the three demon kings so tightly that not even water could have passed through. The eldest demon lost his head in panic and cried, “Brothers, this is terrible! That monkey is truly a devil of cunning. Where did he find such a mighty patron?” The third demon said, “Elder Brother, do not be frightened. Let us charge forward together, strike down the Tathagata with spear and sword, and seize his precious Thunderclap Monastery.” Knowing neither his place nor the odds against him, that demon truly raised his blade, charged forward, and hacked wildly. But Manjusri and Samantabhadra recited their true spells and shouted, “You sinful beast! Why do you still not return to the righteous path? What are you waiting for?” The eldest and second demons were so terrified that they dared resist no longer. Dropping their weapons, they rolled over and revealed their true forms. The two bodhisattvas cast their lotus thrones onto the monsters’ backs, flew up, and mounted them; thus the two demons meekly submitted and took refuge.

Then the three honored Buddhas of Past, Future, and Present, together with five hundred arhats and three thousand guardian deities, spread out to either side and surrounded the three demon kings so tightly that not even water could have passed through.

p.src: Once the two bodhisattvas had subdued the Azure Lion and the White Elephant, only the third demon still refused to submit. Spreading his wings, he cast aside his halberd, soared straight upward on the whirlwind, and reached out with his sharp talons to seize the Monkey King. But the Great Sage was hidden within the radiance, and the demon dared not draw near. The Tathagata understood his intent. He flashed his golden light and, facing the wind, gave a shake of the head crowned by his ushnisha, transforming it into a fresh, crimson lump of flesh. The fiend struck at it once with his sharp talons. The Buddha pointed one hand upward, and the sinews in the demon’s wings instantly stiffened. Unable to fly away, he remained trapped atop the Buddha’s crown, incapable of escaping far. There he revealed his true form: the great golden-winged Peng eagle. He opened his beak and called out to the Buddha, “Tathagata, why have you used your great divine power to imprison me?” The Tathagata replied, “You have committed countless sins in this place. Come with me, and you shall have the chance to advance in merit.” The fiend said, “Where you dwell, everyone fasts and eats vegetarian fare, living in utter poverty and hardship; here I eat human flesh and enjoy pleasures without end. If you let me starve to death, the sin will be yours.” The Tathagata said, “I preside over the four great continents, and countless beings look up to me. Whenever they perform a good deed, I shall have them offer food to you first.” The great Peng wished to break free but could not, and wished to flee but had no way to do so. With no other choice, he submitted and took refuge.

p.src: Only then did the Pilgrim emerge. Bowing his head to the Tathagata, he said, “Venerable Buddha, now you have subdued the fiends and rid the world of a great evil, but my master is gone.” Grinding his teeth with hatred, the great Peng said, “You wretched monkey! You found such a ruthless master to trap me. When was that old monk of yours ever eaten? Is he not now inside the iron chest in the Brocade Fragrance Pavilion?” Hearing this, the Pilgrim hurriedly kowtowed and thanked the Buddha. The Buddha dared not release the great Peng, but ordered him to remain amid the radiant flames as a guardian of the Dharma. Then he led the multitude back upon the clouds and returned directly to his precious monastery.

p.src: The Pilgrim lowered his cloud and went straight into the city, where not a single little fiend remained. Truly, a snake without a head cannot crawl, and a bird without wings cannot fly. When they saw that the Buddha had subdued the demon kings, they had all fled for their lives. The Pilgrim then freed Eight Rules and Friar Sand, found the luggage and the horse, and told the two of them, “Master was not eaten. Follow me.” He led them straight into the inner courtyard and found the Brocade Fragrance Pavilion. When they opened the door, they saw an iron chest inside, from which they could hear Tripitaka weeping. Friar Sand smashed open the iron lock with his demon-quelling staff, lifted the lid of the chest, and called, “Master!” When Tripitaka saw them, he burst into loud sobs and said, “My disciples, how did you subdue the demons? And how did you manage to find me here?” The Pilgrim recounted everything that had happened from beginning to end in full detail. Tripitaka could not thank him enough. Master and disciples found some rice and grain in the palace, prepared tea and a meal, and ate their fill. Then they packed their belongings, left the city, found the main road, and headed west. Indeed:
